CHIEF COMPLAINT
Big toe pain and redness for two weeks, worsening over the past week.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a male presenting with pain and redness in his right big toe that has been present off and on for approximately two weeks, with significant worsening last week during a trade show convention where he was unable to walk the halls comfortably. He describes the pain as throbbing in nature with occasional sharp, stabbing pain, particularly with movement or prolonged walking. He reports walking on his heel to minimize bending of the toe. Patient denies a specific traumatic injury but became concerned when the toe became red and warm to the touch. Pain is exacerbated by light pressure, including contact with bed sheets at night. He has attempted conservative management with ibuprofen 200 mg twice daily without significant relief. Pain worsens with downward motion of the toe more than upward motion. Patient denies relief with bike riding as he pedals with the back of his feet. Patient is generally active, enjoys biking on trails (over 800 miles last year) and is also a runner.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient reports pain with range of motion of the big toe joint, particularly with plantar flexion. He notes sensation of grinding with movement of the joint. Pain with palpation on the lateral aspect of the big toe. Denies stomach problems despite enjoying spicy foods. Denies other systemic complaints.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
None documented.

MEDICATIONS
Ibuprofen 200 mg twice daily (over-the-counter, patient-initiated).

ALLERGIES
Not documented.

FAMILY HISTORY
Not documented.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient works a job requiring standing on his feet daily. He is active with biking (800+ miles annually on trails) and running. He enjoys fishing. He typically wears flip-flops most of the time and uses regular shoes with regular pedals when biking. He enjoys spicy Mexican food.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Inspection reveals redness and warmth of the big toe. Palpation reveals tenderness with a palpable bone spur on the dorsal aspect of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Range of motion testing shows approximately 10 degrees of plantar flexion with pain, increasing to 20 degrees with greater pain. Dorsiflexion causes pain but less than plantarflexion. Joint feels as if there is grinding with movement. Tenderness elicited with medial-lateral compression and movement of the joint. Palpable tenderness on the lateral aspect of the big toe and first metatarsophalangeal joint. Pain with palpation between big toe and second toe, but more pronounced on the lateral aspect.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right foot shows a large bone spur on the dorsal aspect of the first metatarsophalangeal joint and significant cartilage loss consistent with degenerative changes.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Hallux rigidus (rigid big toe joint) with first metatarsophalangeal joint osteoarthritis.

Plan:
1. Orthotic insert for shoe to reduce motion and pain.
2. Start meloxicam (NSAID) once daily for anti-inflammatory effect. Patient counseled to watch for gastric irritation including heartburn or epigastric pain, and to discontinue medication and call if these symptoms develop.
3. Continue regular activities and work to assess treatment efficacy.
4. Follow-up appointment in two weeks to assess response to conservative treatment.
5. If no significant improvement in two weeks, will consider more invasive interventions including intra-articular injection or surgical options such as joint debridement or fusion procedure.
